title: 第10章 瘟疫
text:
Deaf Granny hugged the pine branch to her chest, grinning like a little girl.

"We'll plant it in the courtyard, and after this no filthy thing will ever dare come knocking at our door!"

By the time the two old people reached home, the sky was pitch black.

Granny ordered Wang San's wife to feed the baby some rice porridge, then dug the hole for the branch with her own two hands. When her own son shuffled over to help, she slapped his hand away.

"Clumsy child. You'd offend Elder Pine." She said it the way other people say careful, you'll spill the kettle — as if angering a pine spirit were the most ordinary hazard in the world.

Strange to say, once the branch was in the ground, the whole little courtyard seemed warmer. The shadows softened. The cold seemed to stand a step farther back than it had before.

In the side shrine, where the incense smoke hung thick around the small altars, a voice muttered out of nowhere: "So the old woman went and called Elder Pine himself back. My word. My word." Eighth Master Chang, cozy among his offerings, was genuinely impressed.

After supper, Deaf Granny got to work.

She unwrapped what Chang Baye had brought back from the mountain — the shed skin of something ancient, layers of it, thin as paper and faintly iridescent, glowing under the oil lamp like the inside of a shell. It smelled of cold stone and old temples. It was warm to the touch.

She wound it around the baby in careful rings, tight and precise, the way no clumsy person could. By the time she finished, every part of him was covered except his eyes, his nose, his mouth. She did not miss even the little thing between his legs.

Then she brushed him all over with pine resin mixed with water she had caught from the sky — rain and snowmelt gathered before it ever touched the earth. Rootless water, the purest kind.

And then she wrapped him in another layer of the shed skin.

Three times she did this. Three full layers, brushed and wound and smoothed. Only then did she sit back and let out a long breath.

"There. Done."

Wang San stared, circled the baby, and studied him from every angle.

"Ma, that was a good-looking child, and now look what you've done to him. He's ugly as sin!"

"He looks like a pumpkin."

Deaf Granny couldn't be bothered with her simple son. She went off to the side shrine to light incense for her spirit courts, one by one, the tiny flames glowing in the dark like a row of watchful eyes.

The family's supper had been plain — thin porridge and strips of pickled vegetables. But the porridge filled the belly, and in those lean years a full belly was more than a lot of people ever managed.

After the meal, Old Man Li took out the jade pendant the dead woman had left and examined it by firelight.

The jade was green so deep it looked about to drip — a stone that would buy a grand house in the capital today. The carving was fine work: on the face, a lingzhi mushroom, the fungus of immortality, curled like a little cloud. Beneath it, four small characters in old seal script.

*Healer of the World.*

On the back, a single large character: **Hua.**

Old Man Li turned the pendant over in his calloused fingers, the gold needle he always carried glinting beside it. It was the seal of a physician's house — and not a small one. A great healing lineage.

"This child's origins are anything but simple."

Deaf Granny sighed, long and heavy.

"If they were simple, someone wouldn't have used the Womb-Transfer Curse to destroy his whole family." Her voice was bitter and old and afraid. "He's tangled in something far too big. We tell no one about him. No one."

Old Man Li nodded again and again.

"To the village, I found him in the mountains while hunting. That's all."

"He should bear the surname Hua," the old woman said. "Born to this many hardships before he even drew breath — let's call him Jiunan. Nine Tribulations."

And so the boy was called Hua Jiunan.

Under the two old people's careful watch, the baby grew, and showed nothing out of the ordinary at all. Only this: having drunk in the shed skin, his body carried a mark like a tattoo — a young dragon, hornless and fierce, coiled tight around the trunk of an old green pine. The dragon proud and restless; the pine patient and unbending.

Only then did Deaf Granny realize that the shed skin Chang Baye had brought back those years ago was no common molt. After that, every time she made offerings to her spirit courts, she quietly gave him a little extra.

This delighted Eighth Master Chang beyond measure. He praised the old woman's good heart to anyone who would listen, and he made her a solemn, private promise: the next time danger came, he absolutely would not run.

At least, he promised, not before the filthy things killed her. After that, all bets were off...

One more thing. Every year, on the fifteenth of the seventh month — Hua Jiunan's birthday, the night of the Ghost Festival, the one night of the year when the dead are permitted to walk among the living — Deaf Granny would take him to wait at the foot of the snow mountain.

Because deep in that night, the Snow Corpse would come.

Seated on the Snow Corpse's broad shoulder was a woman — the woman who had given birth to Hua Jiunan and died doing it. The ice had frozen her fast to the creature's body long ago, fused there like a growth. Her face showed clear through the ice: eyes closed, expression peaceful, skin blue-white, frost crystals catching the moonlight. Her hair hung frozen in a single direction, as if a wind had caught it years ago and never let go.

The boy would kowtow to his mother. And the Snow Corpse's crude, half-formed face would shift into a stiff, foolish smile.

Then it would leave behind its gift — a few century-old ginseng roots, or a snow lotus, treasures worth more than the whole village, held out by a dead mother's frozen hands. Deaf Granny received them the way other people receive gold, with hands that weren't quite steady.

The Snow Corpse would stand there, unmoving, until it had watched the old woman carry the boy out of sight. Only then did it turn back into the deep mountains.

Hua Jiunan was too young to think any of it strange.

Every child has a mother. His just lived in the deep mountains, with a big uncle.

Things turned strange again the year he was five.

That year, plague broke out in the little mountain village. In a short time, nearly half the people were down with it. The sick burned hot and then shivered cold; they vomited and purged until, after a few days of it, they were wasted to skeletons. More than a few of the old ones died.

Old Man Li watched and fretted, pressing Deaf Granny day after day to do something.

She wanted to. But she was a Chuma spirit medium, not a doctor. She could cure the sicknesses that spirits caused — the fevers that came from haunting, the wasting that came from a curse, the madness that came from something riding a person's back. But this was flesh-sickness. Real disease, in real blood and bone. For that, her spirits had no answer at all.

So in her desperation she tried the only tools she had. Using the dried well in front of Old Fourth Tian's gate as its center, she laid out an old feng shui arrangement called Eight Winds — objects set in a radiating circle around the dark mouth of the well, like spokes around a hub — and prayed it would blow the village's bad luck away.

It looked like what it was: an old woman's last, small tool against something enormous.

The plague dragged on half a month. More and more people fell. Even the doctor the villagers sent for from the town was helpless.

Then one day, Wang San — the strongest man in the household — went down with it too. And his case was worse than anyone's. He sank into unconsciousness fast, burning up, raving nonsense through cracked lips.

Deaf Granny wept from morning to night.

"San, my San, you can't be hard-hearted like your two brothers. You can't leave your old mother alone and go."

But plague or no plague, the days had to be lived.

Old Man Li still took Hua Jiunan up the mountain every day to tend the forest, and picked up whatever wild game the trail offered, to build Wang San's strength back up.

Li walked ahead. The boy came waddling behind, bundled so thick in hand-stitched cotton padding that he was wider than he was tall — a round little dumpling in faded grey cloth. His legs were too short for the knee-deep snow. Now and then he went down, but he never hit the ground — he just rolled, bouncing softly through the powder like a ball, arms and legs sticking out at angles, rolling on and on, perfectly unharmed.

And at the sight of him, Old Man Li cracked one of his rare smiles.

Joy, stolen from grief. It had to do.

title: 第171章 天地不公
text:
Grey Sixth didn't tell Hua Jiunan any of that — the bitterness, the old wounds.

He only thought it, quietly, to himself:

All of that is over now.

With the Little Master showing us mercy, our family need never again crawl like stray dogs, tails wagging for scraps, swallowing other people's contempt...

For his part, Hua Jiunan had long since taken Grey Sixth as a true brother, blood or not. So he didn't stand on ceremony.

He took the Daoist scripture, flipped through it once, idly — and that was enough. The foundational knowledge recorded there settled into his memory like water into dry ground.

"Sixth Brother, I've got it all. Here's the book back."

"The young ones in the family are just starting their training — this'll serve them fine for building a foundation."

"Though it's incomplete."

"If a chance ever comes, we should find the second half."

Grey Sixth was still down in the old memories, unable to climb out, and it showed on his face — a certain heaviness. He nodded slowly, took the scripture back, and stowed it against his body with the care of a man putting away his grandmother's ring.

Hua Jiunan saw that look and read it wrong.

He thought for a moment, then said, "Sixth Brother — the breathing, the inner circulation, the... dragon-tiger binding I passed to you, you can hand down to our family's children and nephews—"

He never finished the sentence.

Weight fell on the yard.

Not wind. Not a blow. Weight — as if the sky had lowered itself a hand's breadth and meant to go lower. Every knee in the courtyard buckled at once. Breathing became labor, each breath like hauling a bucket up from a deep well. There was no source, no direction, no enemy to see. Only gravity itself, grown heavier, the way air grows heavy in a courtroom when the judge walks in.

Even Zhao Fei, ordinary human flesh that he was, felt it. He stood there gasping, sucking air, turning in a confused circle.

"We were fine a second ago — the hell is happening..."

Eighth Master Chang said not one word. He simply coiled — fast, practiced, a big body folding itself small in one motion — and buried his head in the center of himself. Nothing to do with me. I know nothing. I have never known anything.

Chen Daji opened his mouth to say something stupid, and Grey Sixth clapped a hand over it.

"You little wretch — keep talking and you'll die for it!"

Having scolded him, Grey Sixth turned and spoke fast, low, urgent.

"Little Master — the mercy you've shown us, the Grey family will remember it unto ten thousand generations!"

"But our blessings are shallow and our roots are thin. We would never dare dream of passing down the Celestial Master's sacred texts, generation to generation!"

"Please — take back your words!"

That is what his mouth said.

His face said something else. The grievance on it was thick enough to spread on bread — the dejection, the loss, the hunger of a creature being offered everything it had ever wanted and watching itself say no. Hua Jiunan saw every bit of it and missed none.

What does a man live for? Simple: so the people he loves can live happy.

Rage went up through Hua Jiunan like a geyser through a crack in the earth.

He had already guessed where the crushing weight came from. He raised his head against it anyway — slowly, like lifting a beam — and held up three fingers to the night sky.

"Three feet above our heads, the gods are watching!"

"Heaven and earth, bear witness: Grey Sixth Brother and I are sworn in blood and fire — he has risked his life for me more times than I can count!"

"The old ones said: kindness unrepaid is no virtue, wrong unavenged is no life!"

"I offer my yin merit and my allotted years — every year of them, and whatever grace I'd have carried into the next world — so that in every generation of the Grey family, three may practice the arts I've passed down!"

Grey Sixth made a sound that wasn't quite a word and dropped — a collapse, not a kneel, both knees striking the packed dirt with a heavy thud.

"Little Master, your kindness is an ocean — the Grey family will carry it in their hearts every generation, not one second forgotten!"

"But this must not be! Please, I beg you, take back your words!"

Then he bowed his head to heaven and earth, again and again. Forehead to dirt, up, forehead to dirt — a dull, rhythmic knocking, his whole body shaking, and the sky above him gave no sign it even noticed.

The small rats hidden all around came out.

Out of cracks in the wall, from under the eaves, from holes in the dark earth — dozens of them, grey and small and trembling. They stood upright on their hind legs and pressed their tiny front paws together, the formal salute, done properly, the way it's supposed to be done. And with tears standing on their little black faces, they bowed to the empty sky, over and over and over.

The weight kept growing.

Zhao Fei went down — flat on the ground, arms shaking, unable to hold himself up.

Chen Daji understood nothing about what was happening. But he understood this much: something was bullying Hua Jiunan and Grey Sixth Brother.

He was a fool most days, that one. But he had never once lacked the courage to die for a friend.

He struggled up under the crushing pressure, got one arm pointing at the sky, and let fly, spit flying off his teeth.

"Goddammit — what's the matter with you?! Bullying people, is that your game?"

"My granny always said: even a killing only costs a bow — once a man's knelt, you let him up! And my granny was never wrong!"

"Grey Sixth Brother has kowtowed his head bloody to you — what more do you want?!"

Still cursing, Chen Daji hauled Grey Sixth up off the ground by main force. The two of them stood together, planted firm, at Hua Jiunan's back.

"Sixth Brother, get up!"

"Begging's no use — fine, then we fight the son of a bitch!"

"Fuck it! Dead or alive, I go down swingin' — come what may!"

And then he punched himself in the nose — hard, a real punch, enough to bring water to his eyes — drew a slingshot from his pocket, a child's thing, a tree fork and a rubber band, and aimed it at heaven.

Grey Sixth, staring at that ridiculous, fearless fool, felt every old humiliation he had ever swallowed come roaring up at once — and he threw back his head and howled.

"Heaven and earth are unjust — fate is unjust — my Grey family will NOT submit!!!"

title: 第602章 地动龙游
text:
Chen Daji needed no second invitation. While Xu Fu stood there tensing up, Chen Daji came on with a mean little grin, one slow step at a time, and the war giants — sensing their new master's mood — closed in from every side.

"Old man Xu, you feeling how hot it's getting in here? Why don't you go wash off in the river, same as Little White?"

He cracked his knuckles. "And while you're down there, catch a few turtles for the pot. Stewed turtle. Nothing better for you."

Xu Fu went rigid.

Wash? Catch turtles?

You want to feed ME to the turtles, you son of a bitch. Or is it the turtles getting fed on ME?

The sheer gall of the man!

His hand had already closed tight around the Eight-Gates Formation Disc without his thinking about it, and he was opening his mouth to say something he'd regret when the ground lurched under his feet.

Not shook. Rolled — the way a ship's deck rolls in heavy weather, and beneath the rolling came a sound like thunder heard through miles of stone, deep enough that it hummed in the chest rather than the ears. Everyone staggered. Dust sifted down out of a clear sky. Something vast, far below, was shifting its weight.

Xu Fu swallowed whatever he'd been about to say and cried out instead.

"Disaster! The earth dragon is turning over — the dragon veins are moving! The gate of the Daoist Cache is going to close!"

Ignorance is its own kind of courage.

Chen Daji pointed at him and roared with laughter. "Look at the old man jump! Ha! His eyelids are fluttering and everything!"

"So the door closes. Big deal — we stay a few extra days. There's food, there's drink, there's fun. What the hell are you scared of?"

Xu Fu couldn't be bothered with the loudmouth hick. Two fingers pressed together like a blade came up and touched the center of his brow, and his lips began moving — too fast to catch single words, the syllables blurring into one low sustained sound. The air around him tightened, the way it does before lightning.

"Souls rise. Seven stars, fix your places. Mystery of the old way — RETURN!"

Then he simply wasn't there. No flash. No sound. One instant he stood among them; the next, the space where he'd been was briefly cold, like a door opened onto winter and shut again.

"Holy shit — the old man ran?!" Chen Daji stood there gaping. But the Celestial Hound, who had already adopted him as a cousin, snapped alert a heartbeat later.

"When the Cache closes, there is no telling when it opens again. The next moment — or a hundred years. A thousand."

"And if we're trapped inside when the veins shift, the dragon veins will suppress us. Devour us."

"You're kidding me. It works like THAT?!" The danger landed all at once, and Chen Daji shot off like a startled cat.

"Move, move, move! Eighth Master! Little White! Jianqiang! We gotta go save my Boss!"

Chang Baye, who worried about Hua Jiunan more than anything under heaven, gave a whistling cry and made for the inner city — and the Celestial Hound slid sideways to block his path.

"There is no time. We leave NOW. Half a breath late, and none of us ever gets out."

It didn't bother dodging the fist Chen Daji swung at it in his panic. Its back split open and two wings unfolded — not feathers but fleshy membranes, veined and dark, spreading with a heavy wet sound like a sail catching wind. Black light poured down. Not light at all: a darkness with weight to it, settling over all of them like a shroud of heavy silk, and inside it the world began to dissolve.

"Dark star, guide us. Souls, return to your places — OBEY!"

The word hit like a door slamming. Amid Chen Daji's stream of curses, the whole company vanished — a snap, like Xu Fu before them, and gone.

At that same moment, in the inner palace of Mo City, Fan Ju felt the Cache shudder.

He went blank for half a heartbeat. Then the corners of his mouth flickered — he caught it, smoothed his face flat with the effort of a man closing a ledger. Only his eyes had brightened, and he let them dim again, deliberately.

So. Heaven's timing favors me.

With the upheaval coming fast, the Young General would have no time to succeed to the Grand Master's seat.

He was far too clever to say any of it aloud. One wrong word and Qin Guxi would turn on him and pin him here for good.

So Fan Ju rose slowly and bowed, deep and respectful, to the Mohist Grand Master.

"I had a hundred questions I longed to trouble you with, elder. But with the dragon veins on the move, I must take my leave — with my regrets. Senior Qin — until we meet again."

Qin Guxi had already felt Chen Daji's departure, and his heart was not in it. His answer came flat, automatic.

"Of course, of course. When the Cache opens again, Chancellor — we'll speak of the art of alliance and strategy."

Fan Ju bowed humbly once more, and bit by bit faded out of the inner palace, a careful smile fixed in place.

Hua Jiunan's thoughts were all with Chen Daji and Chang Baye. He was opening his mouth to go find them when Qin Guxi sighed and spoke first.

"Crown Prince, don't fret yourself. They're already clear of Mo City under the Celestial Hound's escort."

He drew something from his robes and held it out. "This is the Grand Master's Seal. When you return to the mortal world, give it to the Young General. Tell him — the day the Daoist Cache opens again is the day he becomes Grand Master."

Hua Jiunan rejoiced for Chen Daji even as he bowed and extended both hands, palms up, to receive it. The token was heavier than it looked — dark metal gone green at the edges, inscribed with characters older than any script still living, and cold as river stone. He was holding, in his two careful hands, the authority of an entire school.

"On behalf of my brother Daji, I thank the Grand Master for his faith in him."

"The earth dragon has turned and the Cache is drifting. If there is nothing else you require of me, elder, I too must beg my leave."

Qin Guxi saw the danger as clearly as anyone, and marveled — even now, with the ground rolling under their feet, the young man did not so much as raise his voice. A prince's composure, bred in the bone. He lifted his hand in a gesture of invitation.

"You're too courteous, Crown Prince. I'll see you out myself."

title: 第1236章 阴阳岛，飞来峰
text:
Chang Baye was already the fastest thing under heaven, and now, spurred on by the rising cheers of the Loiterer Legion's four household heads, he ran like the devil himself was chasing him.

Only the seating arrangement said everything about rank:

The top three rode on Eighth Master's back. Old Fourth Xin was wrapped in the tail.

Not that Grand Warden Xin Lianshan felt the least bit shamed by it.

This was a King Equal to the Throne of the Lineage of the Perfected — the Lord of Ten Thousand Snakes! A being who stood at the same height as the sovereign himself.

Most folk would beg a lifetime just to be coiled by him, and he wouldn't bother to glance at them.

Guided by Granny Hemp-Mourning's senses, the group tore along for nearly a hundred kilometers.

Chen Daji, who'd been soothing Little Diplomas, suddenly spoke up.

"Boss! Boss! Why does this place look so damn familiar?"

"Isn't this where we ran into Sea Uncle... only the island got carted off on that Great Turtle's back!"

Hua Jiunan looked hard, and sure enough — it was exactly that.

He silently admired Chen Daji. The man had been a hundred-battle general in a past life; even half a vat of Granny Meng's Tea of Forgetfulness hadn't dulled his sense of space.

Then, as they talked, thick fog came pouring out of the sea all around them.

It rose the way breath rises off deep water — from below, not from the horizon, grey-white and reeking of salt and something older. In seconds the world was gone. Hua Jiunan couldn't see his own hand in front of his face, and the sound of the sea vanished, replaced by a muffled silence that pressed in on his eardrums like water.

"Holy shit, we've got ghosts?!"

That Chen fellow whipped his head around, left and right.

He did, after all, still have one small goal in life — catch himself a ghost and raise it like a pet.

Granny Hemp-Mourning cackled around her pipe stem.

"Heh heh heh, you little wretch, are you stupid or what?"

"With us grandma-and-grandkids here, what ghost would be dumb enough to come looking for death?"

"You drink too much of that bootleg swill?"

At that, the Grand Warden, still wrapped in the great tail, sheepishly lowered his bottle.

The label read CHRYsANTHEMUM VILLAGE in gaudy painted flowers, the liquor inside a suspicious yellowish color, and a chemical-sweet stench rolled off it and hit everyone at once...

"Your Grace, Blessed Orthodox Deity, ma'am, you don't understand — the fake stuff gives you a splitting headache, but it's cheap."

"That old bastard driving the truck clean ruined me. It was only after I took that hired-mourning gig for old man Liu — wailing at his funeral for pay — that the Little Master's reward finally let me pay off my debts..."

Seeing Grand Warden Xin Lianshan looking so pitiful, like a scolded dog, Granny Hemp-Mourning softened a little.

"That was this old woman's failing. I've been a poor host."

"When we get back, I'll send General Xin home with some of the Ten-Fruit Wine I've had aging in Hemp-Mourning Mountain for a hundred years. He can sip on it slow."

Never mind the warden showering her with a thousand thanks. At the words "driving the truck," Hua Jiunan's thoughts went straight to Mo Huang.

So the Mohist Sovereign had "tricked" Granny Hemp-Mourning into coming to Yuhang — again?

Only that man could get the Underworld itself to "cooperate with an operation," and only he had that much idle time on his hands. A god who treats the mortal world as his playground — every deed looks like aimless fun, but there's always a knife of purpose hidden underneath.

What did he want with Nana, exactly...

He was still turning it over when a wind came off the water — cold straight to the marrow, cold like the light in a room where someone has just died.

Then Sea God Island appeared ahead of them, little by little.

Not clearing out of the fog. Drifting out of a mirror — a reflection becoming solid, first a shimmer, then edges, then mass, sliding across from somewhere that was not here.

And this Sea God Island was nothing like the living green they had known. Every leaf was the color of ash. Not a bird, not an insect, not a breath of wind moved on it, and the sea around it lay flat and dead as oil on a pond. A faint dark haze clung to its surface, like mold on bread. It was wrapped end to end in death.

"No — that can't be — a Yin-Yang Island?!"

Xin Lianshan, giddy with the promise of fine wine only moments before, went white with terror.

"Say, uh, Young General — I'm just gonna head home and shave my leg hair, alright?..."

The Grand Warden tried to desert on the spot. But he was still wrapped tight in Chang Baye's great tail, and could do nothing but blink his huge, innocent eyes at Hua Jiunan, pleading.

Hua Jiunan was the Emperor of Devotion, but he was no fool.

A moment this critical — no way was he letting his only guide who knew the road slip away.

He gave a dry cough, pretended to read none of it, and asked with a sunny smile:

"General Xin — what's a Yin-Yang Island? Tell me all about it, would you?"

Xin Lianshan would happily bullshitchat with Chen Daji all day, but he wouldn't dare show Hua Jiunan the slightest disrespect.

He swallowed his panic and explained.

"Little Master — you haven't broken through the womb-veil yet. Every reborn soul carries it, that forgetting that comes with a new body, so there's a lot of strange stuff you can't remember."

"A Yin-Yang Island is a place that drifts between the world of the living and the world of the dead. Like a door left ajar between two rooms — it belongs to neither. The legendary immortal lands across the sea, the Three Isles and Ten Continents — they're all things of that kind."

At this the Child Ghost frowned his pale silver eyebrows and slowly shook his head.

"The Three Isles and Ten Continents were never immortal lands to begin with. They were the Flown-Here Peaks."

"Only after our Lineage of the Perfected joined with the Patchwork God lineage and 'purified' them did the so-called 'immortals' move in — squatters on seized ground."

"Before that — even 'immortals' didn't dare go NEAR them!!"

Hua Jiunan felt the ground shift beneath everything he knew. The jade palaces, the peach gardens — all of it sat on top of something older and uglier, the way fine paint sits over rot. Conquered, cleaned, and called paradise.

title: 第1798章 你俩给我等着
text:
Cornered with no way out, Chen Fu's voice shook as he bargained.

"Look, General Xin — if it weren't for these two kids, I'd let you kill me myself. Gladly."

"But they're still so young..."

The Grand Warden was rough around the edges but not stupid, and he worried Chen Fu might hold this against him later. He hurried to explain.

"Master Chen, rest easy — I never once thought of it!"

"You and the two young masters just stand there and watch. I'll hold out as long as I can hold out."

"If it truly comes to it, we die together — all of us! And the Little Master and the Young General will avenge us!"

That was the speech. The thoughts underneath it ran differently.

If this damned Bone Arena kills me, I might just get enshrined by Radiant Lady Guanghua — promoted to the ranks of the divine. Bad luck turned good, just like that.

But if I lay a finger on Master Chen myself... Enshrined? Enshrined my ass.

Even if they ground me down to a ghost's ghost — the shriveled husk that's left when even a spirit dies — the Young General would find a way to haul me back up and torture me three hundred and sixty different ways.

So the choice was obvious. I'm not an idiot...

While the Grand Warden threw himself against the sixteen colossal bone beasts that had just crawled out of the dark — bone grinding against bone, a dozen skeletons moving at once, his form flickering like a candle in wind — Zhao Fei and Zhang Chao were not idle either.

Zhao Fei leaned close to Zhang Chao's ear and whispered.

"Chao'er, hurry up and get your family's relative out of that coffin — ain't nobody holding it down anymore!"

He didn't need to say it. Zhang Chao had been straining the whole time.

You only had to look at him: jaw clenched, face beet-red, veins standing out on his forehead, his whole body pushing against something that would not move — exactly like a man badly constipated.

"Boss Zhao, I know! It's always a hair short — it just won't come out!"

"Blood. The thing in the coffin needs blood! We're one drop short!"

"Blood?" That one stumped Zhao Fei.

If he weren't trapped in the Bone Arena, he'd have cracked his own head open on the coffin lid to make up the difference. But now...

Right at that moment, a plump crow — oily black feathers, one dark eye fixed downward — caught the scent of death below and began circling lazily over their heads.

Zhao Fei's big eyes rolled. He had an idea.

"Say, Chao'er — it doesn't have to be human blood, right? Animal blood work?"

Zhang Chao, purple from straining, blinked. Then, uncertainly:

"Should... should work, I guess."

"I get the feeling the fella in there... the Boss isn't a picky eater anymore."

"And I don't know why, but I'm scared of him. Really, really scared."

There was no time — Zhao Fei didn't hear a word after "animal."

"Oh! Animal blood I can handle!"

He put on a face of pure delighted surprise, stared straight up at the crow, and hollered:

"Bird Bro! Bird Bro, you came?! We're down here!!"

"Run, quick — go tell Boss Hua and my master the bad guys are gonna kill us!"

The fat kid's shout startled the crow — and it startled the so-called High Envoy even more.

As the Bone Shaman's trusted confidant, of course he knew of Hua Jiunan.

That was Emperor Tingmeng, the terror of the ancient world!

And there was a proverb the old survivors passed mouth to mouth, one the High Envoy had learned by rote as a child and could never forget. His hand tightened on his bone staff. His breath caught.

"Meet Three-Face, and life and death hang unresolved; meet Tingmeng, and misfortune is all you'll find."

And — do you remember the Blood-Colored Sea?!

So when the bird overhead turned out to be an enemy spy, the High Envoy didn't hesitate for half a heartbeat. He grinned, swept up his ritual staff, and loosed a bone arrow at the crow.

A full-power strike from the High Envoy — even the Grand Warden couldn't take one head-on. Let alone an "ordinary" crow.

The arrow punched through its chest with a wet, meaty crack. The bird-scream cut short. The crow tumbled out of the air and landed with a heavy thud — square on the coffin lid.

Blood sprayed hot and bright from the wound, and the coffin drank it. The wood darkened and soaked it up impossibly fast, like parched earth drinking rain, while the crow's feathers matted red and its body twitched.

What nobody expected: this crow was no ordinary crow. Dying, its little eyes glared hard at the High Envoy and Fatty Zhao.

"F-fuck's sake. I go out to find a quiet spot to take a shit, and you two screw Big Bro over?"

"Just you wait, both of you. This ain't over!"

Then its legs kicked out, it screeched once, and it died unwilling.

Zhao Fei: "......"

"Did... did I just screw up bad?"

"That wasn't Feather Bro's... Feather Sis's — (the Solar Luminary, the little crow Black Feather) — relative, was it?!"

But Zhang Chao was at the critical moment and had no time for him.

Every muscle in his body straining, he shouted with all the strength he had:

"The Northern Dipper holds death — the Southern Dipper holds life! By the Jade Emperor's mandate, I command you: rise and walk!"

"Come out — B-Boss Chen!"

The words landed like a gavel. The air pressure dropped. The coffin wood groaned, and something inside shifted.

Then Zhang Chao stood there, blinking at the coffin, genuinely puzzled.

"Why the hell did I shout 'Boss Chen'?"

title: 第2297章 人不散（大结局）
text:
Nobody knew how much time had passed — but here it was, the last winter break of college for Hua Jiunan and Chen Daji.

They'd been held up by some business or other, so the two of them didn't make it home until New Year's Day itself, and the sky was already going dark when the train pulled in.

Waiting on the platform to meet them — to their utter delight — was Chen Fu.

So many years had passed. Chen Daji had changed, grown steadier. But the moment he laid eyes on his long-lost father, all that steadiness evaporated into pure, howling joy.

"HOLY SHIT, DAD, YOU'RE ALIVE?! You got OUT of the chessboard?!"

"Mom's finally not a widow anymore!"

"One more month stuck in there and I was gonna talk her into remarrying!"

Chen Fu, who had been just as thrilled to see his son, promptly ignored the crowd of onlookers at the station and demonstrated the time-honored art of 'the rod of filial education' — he beat the living daylights out of the little menace right there on the platform.

If Hua Jiunan hadn't grabbed him, this freshly reunited father and son would have been parted again by untimely death.

From the car came the Big Han's hearty laughter as he watched the menace's sorry, bruised state.

Hua Jiunan hurried over, bowing with a smile, greeting him softly: "Old Ancestor, it's been a long time."

The Big Han nodded along, all simple good humor. "Mm, mm, mm, long time, long time."

"Little Nine, you and Daji both doing well... well, Daji there doesn't count as doing well. Poor kid. Hahaha!"

That Chen fellow shuffled over too, sniffling.

"Old Ancestor, why didn't you get out of the car and pull my dad off me?"

"Geez, he nearly beat me to death... was it you who brought Dad back to life?"

"Fished him out of that little chessboard?"

At the mention of his own achievement, the Big Han's face filled with modest pride.

"You bet it was me!"

"Not just Chen Fu, either. I brought back everyone!"

"Except those two weasels — they wanted divine titles, so Little Nine's mom officially elevated them into the Radiant Lady's mansion."

Hearing all this, the little menace suddenly remembered that his godmother still had a whole shelf of divine titles to hand out.

He stuck his thumb up at the Big Han. "An old person in the house is a treasure in the house. Old Ancestor, you're the best!"

Under this barrage of flattery, the Big Han promptly got carried away, nodding like a chicken pecking rice.

"That's right! Didn't I always say it? Your Old Ancestor is old, not dead — would I ever let the descendants take a loss?!"

"Heh heh!"

Just then, Elder Ghost came walking over with the Yellow Family Ancestor in tow. He didn't say a word to anyone else — he went straight to the old weasel.

"Little Huang, you see this? This is exactly how they wore me down, back in the day."

"Beat the small ones, then the big ones come."

"And once you've finally killed the big ones and the small ones both, out come the ANCIENT ones."

"The ancient ones are fairly reasonable, I suppose — they don't personally strike. They just infinitely resurrect the big ones and the small ones... How is an outsider supposed to fight that..."

Everyone roared with laughter at Elder Ghost's bitter expression.

Of course, ordinary people couldn't see any of this.

Amid the laughter, Chen Fu drove everyone back to the little courtyard. From far off you could already see the New Year couplets pasted by the gate:

*Heaven and earth in harmony, the family line flourishing;*

*Peace and good fortune, the whole household reunited.*

Banner: **ONE HAPPY FAMILY**.

The moment they stepped through the gate, the Master of Wanlong Mountain and Bai Wuwei came out to greet them.

Hua Jiunan stepped forward, and before either of the two family heads could speak, he said warmly, "Big Brother Bai, you've come back too!"

Bai Wuwei nodded over and over, moved. "It was all thanks to the Human Ancestor's mercy, all thanks to Radiant Lady Guanghua's grace!"

"Master — forgive my presumption — I begged the Lady for a divine title."

"So that I might last longer in this world. Read more medical texts. Help more of the poor."

"I took the liberty without asking. I beg your punishment!"

Hua Jiunan had always been generous with good people — and this was a great physician whose loyalty was absolute and whose heart held no selfishness at all.

He clapped Bai Wuwei on the shoulder three times, smiling. "There. Punishment delivered."

"Come on inside, Big Brother Bai — don't keep Grandma and Nana waiting."

Bai Wuwei's smile turned mysterious. "Master, it isn't only the two elders waiting. General Li has returned as well!"

Meanwhile, on the other side, that Chen fellow was bouncing around Zhang Shizu.

"Hahaha, Chao'er's ancestor, you're alive too?! Did the Old Ancestor fish you back as well?!"

Feeling the menace's completely genuine joy, Zhang Shizu didn't know what to feel. He kept a careful distance and answered, a little aggrieved:

"My nemesis... Young General — this old body is a special case. This time I didn't trouble the Human Ancestor."

"Have you forgotten I'm a Strange Corpse? I climbed back out of the underworld on my own. Inch by inch."

"Then I gathered my body back together, piece by piece... where pieces were missing, I stitched and patched. Good enough to use..."

That Chen fellow stared. "Ho— holy shit, that WORKS?"

"Chao'er's ancestor, tell me the truth. You're a Transformer, aren't you?"

"You can repair YOURSELF?!"

The exchange set the whole crowd off again.

In the middle of the laughter, Hua Jiunan flicked his sleeve, and every missing and mended part of the Ancestor of Corpse-Herders' body was made whole — along with plenty of other gifts besides.

Zhang Shizu felt it, and ecstasy broke across his face. He moved to bow in gratitude, but Hua Jiunan stopped him — and simply pointed at the banner over the gate.

Zhang Shizu froze. Then his eyes filled with tears. "One Happy Family... Yes. Little Master, Zhang Shizu understands!"

Inside the gate, they found Chang Baye toddling back and forth, helping Chan Third haul things.

The moment the little serpent spotted Hua Jiunan, he came flying — well, crawling at flying speed — and shot up onto Hua Jiunan's wrist with a *whoosh*.

"Little Master, you're home! Little Eight missed you SO much!"

"I- I wanted to go meet you, I really did, but- but Master Chen insisted on going himself."

"Little Eight didn't want to fight with the Master over it, so I just did chores around here and waited."

Hua Jiunan stroked the little serpent's head, his voice gentle. "I know, Eighth Master. It's fine."

Just then, the Shameless Cocoon and Grand Warden Xin Lianshan came through the door, flanking Radiant Lady Guanghua and the Snow Corpse on either side.

The grand warden had finally gotten his wish — transferred to the Radiant Lady's mansion as the "Commanding Deity of the Imperial Guards." In the old ranking, that was a second-rank official, the kind of post only the emperor's most trusted favorite held. So Xin Lianshan these days was one swaggering, preening sight.

The moment he saw Hua Jiunan and Chen Daji, he asked the Snow Corpse's permission, then came waddling over at top speed, big rear end swinging.

"Hahaha, Master, Young General, you're home!"

"Old Xin missed you somethin' awful!"

"Old Xin's doing just fine, don't you worry about me!"

The little menace grimaced. "Who's worried about y—"

Firecrackers drowned out the rest, going off all around them. Everyone froze — then burst out laughing together, shouting as one: "HAPPY NEW YEAR!"

And in that moment of national celebration, Wang San, little Qianyue, and the Fox Maiden came out supporting Deaf Granny and Uncle Li on either arm.

And behind them, shy as ever, came Little Wuxin.

"Homage to Amitabha — big brother!"


---

**Outside the book:** I set down the final word and couldn't bring myself to lift the pen. Everything is still right before my eyes; all the old friends crowd my heart. I had a thousand things to say, and none of them would come. So let the thousands become twelve: *may the song end but the people never scatter; may all my old friends be safe.* Take care of yourselves, every one of you. The mountains are high and the roads long — but I believe we will meet again.

(I shamelessly beg once more for love-powered support. Thank you for never leaving. My new book, *After the Forbidden One*, has resumed updates — eight thousand words a day. In that book, that Chen fellow, the Dragon Lord Chang Huaiyuan, the Rat Clan Patriarch, Little Wuxin and the others all appear, one after another, as legendary figures — a sequel of sorts, set twenty-two years after this book's timeline.)


---

**EXTRAS — the stories that followed, and every lingering regret set right**

East of the azure sea, above the Abyss of Returning Waters, stood an immortal mountain called Returning Home.

At its summit, Hua Jiunan sat with a green qin across his knees, playing the tune "Moonfall and Sinking Stars." Behind him, eight swords wheeled through the air. Before him, the Fox Maiden moved with the wind, her Rainbow-Feathered Robes revealed to the world once more.

Across from him, the Incense Master smiled like a flower and raised her cup again and again. And behind her — ahem — that Chen fellow was craning his neck in every direction, curiosity all over his face, while the great serpent, a black pot perched on its head, lay coiled obediently at Hua Jiunan's feet.

Little Wuxin remained perfectly well-behaved, peeking up shyly now and then — and whenever no one was looking, secretly stuffing a spicy strip into his mouth. Swallow, peek again, eat again, murmur shyly, "Homage to Amitabha."

When the song ended, the Chen fellow, who'd been holding it in forever, finally spoke with an ingratiating grin.

"Boss, you play beautifully. Fei'er dances beautifully... Auntie Incense Master drinks FAST..."

The Incense Master chuckled. "You brat — if you know I drink fast, get over here and pour."

"Coming, coming!" Before his elders, that Chen fellow was always obedient. He trotted over on his bandy legs.

"Auntie, is this the Yellow Emperor's wine? Never had it, wouldn't know the taste, heh heh!"

The Absolute Sage, that woman Emperor, watched him cringe and grovel and laughed all the harder.

"Brat, if you want wine, just say so. Would your auntie stop you?"

"Your auntie isn't stingy like a certain Old Ancestor."

At that, the Big Han — who had just half-materialized — found himself in an awkward spot. Retreat now, and he'd confirmed his stinginess for all time. Stay and answer back... but she was telling the truth.

Luckily, Jiang Chudi, following right behind him, failed to brake and bumped him from behind. The Big Han rode the momentum and appeared fully, looking sheepish.

Everyone rose at once. "We pay our respects to the Old Ancestor!"

The Big Han waved a hand — everyone carry on, no need for ceremony — then plopped down beside the Incense Master.

"Ahem. Xiang'er, it's not that your Old Ancestor is stingy — I left in a hurry and forgot my wine. Just a little of yours..."

At this, Jiang Chudi — thick-built since childhood — didn't react at all. But Emperor Zhuanxu — clever since childhood — hurriedly lowered his head.

The Incense Master was far too wise to argue with the Big Han to his face. She refilled his cup, all smiles, and said — half joking, absolutely not joking —

"Drink as you please, Old Ancestor."

"But let's agree in advance: every cup, you pay back tenfold."

The Big Han froze stone-still, the raised cup neither drinkable nor settable down. His expression changed several times — then he gave Jiang Chudi a light kick in the rear.

"What'd you gotta grow so big and solid for?! If you hadn't bumped me, I— I'd have gone home to bed already!"

Jiang Chudi, a proud one, plainly hadn't understood any of it and wore pure bewilderment. Emperor Zhuanxu pressed his head even lower.

But even that wasn't enough — the Big Han wasn't letting the clever one off.

"What are you laughing at? Thought of names for the Grey Clan whelps yet? I'll have you know his family spawned another hundred-plus litters last month!"

As everyone knows, laughter is transferable. Behold: everyone was laughing now except Emperor Zhuanxu.

That Chen fellow, chuckling, carefully sidled over to the Big Han and started kneading his shoulders with small grimy hands.

"Geez, Old Ancestor, you're so domineering, taking it out on other people."

"I gotta learn from you, truly!"

"So, uh — hey, Old Ancestor, could you beat up my dad sometime? He's always wailing on me and I can't win!"

The Big Han adored the kid and burst out laughing. "You bet!"

"Oh, right — Old Ancestor likes you. Come live with me at the ancestral mountain a few years!"

That Chen fellow lit up instantly. "Deal! As long as there's no school, I'll do anything!"

And at the very moment he agreed — far away at the Ancestral Mountain, the Great Golden Ones were suddenly seized with nameless dread, as if calamity were about to fall. They dropped everything and sat down in perfect unison, eyes closed, divining furiously. They sat down SO neatly that the ground trembled. Anyone who didn't know better would have assumed it was a collective fart.

Amid the merriment, Jiang Chudi asked Hua Jiunan quietly, "Little Nine — Changsheng's guardian was clearly you. So why, in the final battle, did it become Wumian instead?"

It wasn't Hua Jiunan who answered, but shy Little Wuxin. The little one first wiped the chili-oil grease from his hands, pressed his palms together, and bowed.

"Homage to Amitabha."

"Big brother took pity on this little monk, fearing I would die young — so long ago he bound his own life to mine."

"Therefore this little monk is also a guardian of Changsheng."

"Ohhh, I see!" Jiang Chudi's face cleared. "So in that battle, when Wumian resolved to perish together with Changsheng, he first severed his own bond with you — that's why you came through unharmed."

"And after the battle, you pulled him back with your own life. That's why your hair has gone white so young."

"Homage to Amitabha — exactly so. Big brother's mercy!" And Little Wuxin ducked shyly behind Hua Jiunan.

After Jiang Chudi's question, Emperor Zhuanxu voiced his own worry. "Little Nine — those two in Bright Heaven and Dark Heaven..."

Hua Jiunan smiled. "Rest easy, Uncle. Each keeps to their post."

"Good." Zhuanxu nodded deeply. "And those otherworld flowers cursed by heaven and earth?"

At the mention of the Flower-Spirit and the Leaf-Spirit, Hua Jiunan sighed softly. "Rest easy, Uncle. I've made arrangements for them too."

"Not only them — Shopkeeper Liu, Xu Fangcao, every last one has a place to come home to."

Seeing that Hua Jiunan had truly thought of everything, Zhuanxu — who had carried the world on his shoulders since the beginning of things — finally let it go.

Just then, a boundless pressure rolled across the mountain: a command token and a war banner, blotting out the sky. The Lord of Arms' Token. The Lord of Arms' Banner.

They circled once and settled gently atop Hua Jiunan's green qin. Chiyou's voice came from within, majestic and cold.

"From this day, Tingmeng shall serve in my stead as Grand Enforcer of this world. Be iron-faced and impartial, without self-regard!"

"Only so are you worthy of the name of the Perfected!"

Hua Jiunan hesitated — then took up the token and the banner.

"The Perfected have no self; the divine achieve nothing; the sages leave no name... Hua Jiunan understands."

"From today, no one at my side may entangle themselves in mortal karma ever again. In all things, live as ordinary people."

His voice wasn't loud — but it rang clearly in the ears of everyone who heard it, wherever in the world they happened to be.

On Wanlong Mountain, Chang Huaiyuan and the other four family heads of the spirit-medium clans bowed low together.

"We obey the Little Master's command!"

The Mohist Sovereign, who had heard it too, looked utterly miserable. He turned, aggrieved, to the Mohist Ma Mingyang, who was glaring daggers at him.

"Old Ma. Does the Master's order include the two of us, or not?"

Ma Mingyang couldn't be bothered to answer. He simply turned his back, cold and proud: "Guess."


---

**EXTRA: So Many Injustices in the World**

Time flew. Twenty years passed in the blink of an eye, and Hua Jiunan turned forty.

Because he had once traded his own life to bring Wuxin back, his temples had gone white long ago. But the white hair didn't age him — it gave him that particular charm of a grown man. In the girls' words these days: a "mature uncle," an uncle full of seasoned charm and a sense of safety.

Compared to him, that Chen fellow hadn't changed much. Time had left its marks on his face, but not on his personality.

It was one in the morning when the wretch crept, tiptoeing, into Chang Baye's room.

The great serpent — honest to his bones, dreaming only of honest work to feed his wife and kids — had spent the whole day planting herbs in the fields. Dead tired, sleeping sound.

That Chen fellow leaned in close and YELLED into his ear.

The serpent nearly convulsed with fright. He shot bolt upright, tail-tip to the floor, standing rigid as a post on the heated brick bed, big innocent eyes blinking, big head swiveling.

"Who's there?! What happened?!"

"Why'd they scream like that?!"

"ASSASSINS! There's assassins!"

The thought of assassins brooked no hesitation. The serpent launched himself ballistic, shot out the window, and streaked straight for Hua Jiunan's room. In the good serpent's heart, the first thought was always his Little Master. Never mind that the Master was now middle-aged. Never mind that the Master had long been unrivaled in all three realms.

But at Hua Jiunan's door, Chang Baye pulled up short.

Not a sound inside. That meant the Master was still asleep. If the Master was asleep, there were no assassins.

The serpent firmly believed that nothing in heaven, earth, or underworld could sneak up on Hua Jiunan in silence — not even the three Human Ancestors themselves!

"Master's fine, that's what matters," he whispered to himself, as quietly as a serpent can whisper.

"Wait. That scream just now... didn't it sound like a certain little wretch?"

"Was the little wretch assassinated?"

"...Eh. If the little wretch dies, he dies. Honestly, dying would make him happier than coming home."

"If he's really dead, there's plenty of time to notify the family tomorrow morning."

Yawning, the serpent turned and toddled back toward his own room.

And that was when Chen Daji's voice rang out, thick with grievance.

"Eighth Master, you hate me THAT much? You're THAT eager for me to die?!"

"King Yama himself told me to stop dying so much — said don't give the underworld extra paperwork!"

"He said if I die and come back again on a whim, he'll have Brother Ox-Horse and Little-Face Brother take me out back and beat me as a group!"

Here that Chen fellow gave his weaselly little giggle. "Last time I died and went back, remember, I hid a dynamite cap in Sharp-Beak's rice cooker — you know, Bird Beak, the Underworld Marshal."

"Geez, the second he plugged it in — BOOM!"

"Blew his sharp beak all crooked. He can open beer bottles with it now!"

Chang Baye sniffed in contempt. "Cut the crap, you little wretch. Since when does the underworld have electricity? Why don't I know about it?"

"Your dad Master Chen paid to run power lines down there?"

"Little ghosts turning a millstone to generate power?!"

Seeing he wasn't believed, that Chen fellow looked wounded.

"My dad didn't wire them up — Uncle Zhong and the others pulled themselves up by their own bootstraps!"

"They generate power with the River of Forgetfulness!"

"And to make sure everything ran smooth, they had Brother Ox-Horse bring back a whole pile of experts from the land of the living!"

"Including that expert — you know, the one who said fresh college graduates should PAY their employers, as tuition!"

"R- really?" Chang Baye wavered. "Good — dragging that old coot down there was the right call. That man was wicked to the bone, talking against his own conscience!"

"His kid works for somebody else and HE pays the boss? Would he agree to that?!"

He stopped, remembering. "Hey, little wretch — what in the hell were you screaming about just now? You nearly scared my vitals loose!"

There was no way that Chen fellow would admit he'd done it purely to scare the serpent — the tail-lashings would scatter his bones. So he got straight to business.

"Eighth Master, remember Chan Third?"

"Few days back he was sleeping buck-naked on the ground, and somebody STEPPED on him. Squashed flat. Both ends!"

"He told me in a dream just now!"

"WHAT?!" Chang Baye gaped. "Chan Third reached Ghost Immortal rank! How does somebody STEP on him?"

"He's a toad! He doesn't even have a vitals-spot!"

Chen Daji shook his head. "Beats me. He didn't say in the dream."

"Just said hurry up and collect his corpse before the great serpent eats it."

"He wants to be buried whole."

Chang Baye: "..."

But the serpent was kind at heart. He immediately let Chen Daji climb onto his back and point the way. Chan Third wasn't a close friend, exactly — but nobody deserved to rot in the open wilds. And a perfectly good toad didn't just die an unclear death like that. Somebody owed somebody an explanation. If it was deliberate — easy, the little wretch would beat the culprit into paste as revenge. And if it was an accident, just somebody passing by — well, they'd still have to apologize to Chan Third and mind their step next time.


---

**EXTRA: A Son of the Chang Family**

Just as Chang Baye was about to head out, a strange egg came drifting out of the room.

(A special note here: this book and *After the Forbidden One* are not the same storyline. Old friends who've read that one — bear with us, and no spoilers.)

This was Chang Baye's son — the son he'd had with the Ying Dragon. His name was Chang Jie.

But like our Eighth Master, he'd been born frail, and only half-hatched. The top half had made it out of the shell. The bottom half was still stuck.

So from a distance, he looked exactly like a rotting egg with a maggot in it.

And that "maggot" had mismatched eyes crossed inward besides, plus two thick heavy eyebrows over them, so that no matter how you looked at him, he looked... wrong.

After "hatching," Chang Jie came drifting slowly toward his father, muttering all the while, aggrieved to his core: "Both my parents are dragons, and I'M a maggot. Where's the justice..."

Before Chang Baye could say a word, the Young General had already scampered over and scooped him up — and got a face-full of protest, Chang Jie pecking kisses all over his little fleshy head, spittle everywhere.

"Geez, Little Jie, why are you out in the middle of the night?"

"Upset stomach? Go poop, then!"

The poor little maggot hung in the Young General's arms, his face the very picture of a life without hope.

Chang Baye whipped his tail and sent that Chen fellow flying, then caught his darling son securely — and said nearly the same words: "Little Jie, you're frail, you shouldn't be out this late. Listen to your dad and go back inside."

"Missing your mom, can't sleep? Where's the pacifier Old Diplomas gave you?"

"Suck on it a while and you'll drop off. Good boy."

"Okay." Chang Jie's voice was boneless with exhaustion. He nodded and drifted back toward the house, muttering as he went: "Both my parents are dragons, and I'M a maggot. Where's the justice..."

He drifted slowly, like a balloon on a windless day. Halfway there, he stopped — and turned around.

Chang Baye was curious. "Little Jie? What is it? Weren't you going to bed?"

Chang Jie sighed. "Dad — the Young General was right. I do have an upset stomach. I was going to the toilet."

"You two distracted me and I forgot."

"Ohhh, I see, I see!" Chang Baye nodded rapidly. "Then go, go!"

"You scared? Want Dad to come with you?"

"Did you bring paper? Bring the soft kind, remember."

"Your hide's too tender — the hard stuff'll scrape you."

As Chang Baye nattered on with worry, the last light of hope dimmed further on his son's already hopeless face. Chang Jie said nothing — just turned and drifted back toward the house, sighing, as if nothing remained in this world worth caring about.

Seeing his son like this, Chang Baye panicked.

"Little Jie, what's wrong?! Did Dad do something?"

"Are you feeling sick somewhere?"

Chang Jie knew how deeply his father loved him, so he answered at top speed for once — instead of his usual glacial pace that could drive a saint mad.

"Don't worry, Dad, it's a small thing."

"I had an upset stomach, then forgot, and then you delayed me — and I pooped in the eggshell."

"So no toilet needed. I'll just go inside and wash my rear end."

Chang Baye: "..."

"Good boy. You've suffered so much..."

By then, the tail-swatted Chen fellow was limping back. "OW, that hurts — Eighth Master, your tail's getting stronger!"

"Good thing it's me. Anybody else'd be whipped into powder!"

Chang Baye still found his best friend insufferable, and sniffed coldly.

"I don't whip anybody else. Only you, you little wretch."

"Now stop dithering. Stay put right there."

"I'm bathing Little Jie first, THEN going to collect Chan Third's corpse."

All the commotion naturally woke the Master. The lamp lit, and his voice came gentle as ever: "Eighth Master, Daji — what's going on out there? Is something the matter? Do you need my help?"

The honest serpent shook his head so hard it was like a rattle-drum, his little tongue flapping.

"No no, Little Master, no need — it's all small stuff."

"So sorry to disturb your rest! Little Eight was wrong!"

With Chang Baye, the Master was gentler still.

"Eighth Master, why are you always so formal with me?"

"Don't worry, you didn't disturb me. Truly, I'm going back to sleep. You and Daji don't stay up too late playing."

"And Little Jie especially — it's cold out, don't let him go outside... Actually, are you scared to sleep alone, Little Jie? Come here, I'll tell you a story and rock you to sleep."

Chang Jie had grown up in the Master's arms. The Master had held him and rocked him more than his own father and the Ying Dragon combined. So of all people, Chang Jie was closest to the Master — and the Master's doting on him was unprecedented and, presumably, never to be matched.

On Chang Jie's first birthday, the Master summoned the God of Fortune, the God of Wealth, the God of Joy — every auspicious deity there was — to bless the child. Beyond the gods, the Old Ancestor came leading every one of the Great Golden Ones. Kuafu the Sun-Chaser came. The goddess Meng Po came. Chiyou the Lord of Arms came uninvited. The Fengdu Emperor came leading the Five Ghost Emperors of the Directions and the entire senior staff of the underworld...

Put it this way: the ceremonies of elevation those dignitaries performed for baby Chang Jie took over an hour. Even Chang Baye's own elevation, back in the day, was a mud speck compared to a cloud.

And even so — Chang Jie was still a "maggot."

If the Master hadn't promised him, word of honor, that one day he would roar like a dragon across the ninth heaven, shake the earth, and startle the whole world with a single move —

the poor kid would have gloomily gone and dashed himself against a marble by then.

One special note: strange as Chang Jie looks, he's staggeringly brilliant. At age one, he had the intelligence of an eighteen-year-old — and not just any eighteen-year-old. The kind who tests into the top national universities.


**Outside the book:** the sequel to this volume is complete — *The Underworld Calls Me Little Master II*. If you've enjoyed this, please keep reading.
